evidence.excerpt: This paper develops a steady-state pricing model for a single-machine make-to-order shop operating under Poisson arrivals and generally distributed service times (M/G/1 queue). The model links the posted price of a job to the current workload level measured in machine-hours, allowing the firm to dampen demand when the queue is long and stimulate it when capacity is idle. A profit function combining contribution margin with holding and tardiness costs is maximised over a finite price grid. Numerical experiments calibrated on data from a small metal-fabrication firm in Vojvodina show that workload-contingent pricing reduces average tardiness by 18% and increases weekly contribution margin by 11% compared with a static price policy. Sensitivity analysis reveals that the benefit of dynamic pricing grows with demand variability and diminishes when the coefficient of variation of service times exceeds 2.0. The paper discusses implementation requirements, including real-time workload visibility and customer acceptance of variable quotes.
